10  Mitosis and Meiosis

Investigating Mitosis, Meiosis, and the Cellular Basis of Genetic Continuity and Variation

10.1 Learning Objectives

By the end of this laboratory, students will be able to:

  1. Identify and distinguish all major phases of mitosis and meiosis.

  2. Explain how chromosome behavior differs between mitosis and meiosis.

  3. Calculate the mitotic index from microscopic observations.

  4. Analyze how meiosis generates genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

  5. Compare chromosome number and DNA content through the cell cycle.

  6. Interpret the biological significance of mitosis and meiosis in growth, repair, reproduction, and evolution. [oercommons.org], [lagccnsdoer.commons.gc.cuny.edu]

10.2 Background

Cell division is essential for growth, tissue repair, and reproduction. During mitosis, one diploid parent cell produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. During meiosis, a diploid germ cell undergoes two divisions to produce four genetically distinct haploid cells. Meiosis introduces genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment. [oercommons.org], [lamc.edu]

10.3 Materials

Microscopy Station

  • Compound light microscope

  • Prepared onion root tip slides

  • Prepared whitefish blastula slides

  • Lens paper

Modeling Station

  • Chromosome modeling kit (pipe cleaners, beads, or chromosome models)

  • Colored pencils or markers

  • Meiosis worksheet

Data Analysis Station

  • Cell counting grid

  • Calculator

  • Graph paper or spreadsheet software

10.4 Safety Considerations

  • Carry microscopes using both hands.

  • Handle glass slides carefully.

  • Keep workstations clean and dry.

  • Wash hands before leaving the laboratory.

10.5 Pre-Lab Questions

  1. What is the difference between homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids?

  2. Define diploid and haploid.

  3. During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?

  4. Why is crossing over important?

  5. Why would chromosome number double every generation if meiosis did not occur?

During this activity you will work in pairs.

10.6 Part I: Microscopic Examination of Mitosis

10.6.1 Procedure

A. Onion Root Tip Observations

  1. Observe the prepared onion root tip slide under low power.

Figure 10.1: Longitudinal section of an Allium (onion) root tip, 40× magnification. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Apical_Meristem_in_Allium_Root_Tip_(23581053848).jpg

  1. Locate the apical meristem region. This is within the zones of division.

Figure 10.2: Main tissues and regions of activity in an onion root tip. https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Main-tissues-and-regions-of-activity-in-an-onion-root-tip-source_fig1_279398426

  1. Switch to high power (400×).

  2. Identify cells in:

    • Interphase

    • Prophase

    • Metaphase

    • Anaphase

    • Telophase

Figure 10.3: Onion root tip cells in various stages of mitosis. https://www.carolina.com/mitosis-meiosis-microscope-slides/onion-mitosis-slide-ls-10-m-quadruple-stain/302408.pr

  1. Draw one representative cell from each stage.

    Interphase, Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase

  2. Record the distinguishing characteristics of each stage.

B. Onion Root Tip Analysis

Figure 10.4: Scan and count cells by using either a horizontal (black line) or vertical (blue line) back-and-forth scanning technique with your eyes.

  1. As you scan the field of view you need to count the number of cells in each stage. Scan different parts of the onion root in three different passes as noted above.

  2. Using the prepared slide, record the number of cells in each phase of the cell cycle. Use the method shown in Figure 10.4 to count the cells. Record your count in a data table like that shown in Table 10.1. Share your data with the class to create a group total count.

10.6.2 Calculating Mitotic Index

\[\text{Mitotic Index} = \frac{\text{Cells in Mitosis}}{\text{Total Cells Counted}} \times 100\]

Where:

Cells in mitosis = Prophase + Metaphase + Anaphase + Telophase

10.6.3 Questions

  1. Which phase was most common?

  2. Based on the percentage of cells observed in each stage, which phase of the cell cycle lasts the longest?

  3. What does the most common phase suggest about cell cycle duration?

  4. Why are root tips ideal for studying mitosis?

10.7.1 Whitefish Blastula Observations

  2. Scan the prepared whitefish blastula slides as indicated in Figure 10.4.

10.8 Part III: Modeling Meiosis

10.8.1 Chromosome Model Activity

Review the stages of meiosis on the Purple Hubbard Models.

Starting Condition

Create a diploid cell (2n = 4) with:

  • Pair 1: Red homologous chromosomes

  • Pair 2: Blue homologous chromosomes

Each chromosome should consist of two sister chromatids.

Sketches Required

Students must draw all of the following stages:

  • Prophase I

  • Metaphase I

  • Anaphase I

  • Telophase I

  • Prophase II

  • Metaphase II

  • Anaphase II

  • Telophase II

  • Final products

Clearly label:

  • Homologous chromosomes

  • Sister chromatids

  • Chiasmata

  • Centromeres

10.8.2 Meiosis I

Model:

  1. Prophase I

    • Synapsis

    • Crossing over

  2. Metaphase I

    • Homologous pairs line up

  3. Anaphase I

    • Homologs separate

  4. Telophase I

    • Two haploid cells produced

Meiosis I Diagrams

Interphase, Prophase I, Metaphase I, Anaphase I, Telophase I

10.8.3 Meiosis II

Model:

  1. Prophase II

  2. Metaphase II

  3. Anaphase II

  4. Telophase II

Meiosis II Diagrams

Prophase II, Metaphase II, Anaphase II, Telophase II

Result: four genetically unique haploid gametes.

10.9 Part IV: Independent Assortment Simulation

10.9.1 Procedure

Using the 2n = 4 model:

  1. Arrange homologous chromosome pairs randomly at metaphase I.

  2. Record resulting gamete combinations.

  3. Repeat 10 times.

10.11 Post-Lab Discussion Questions

  1. Why must DNA replication occur before both mitosis and meiosis?

  2. Explain why meiosis I is considered a reduction division.

  3. Which meiotic event contributes most to genetic diversity?

  4. How could errors during meiosis lead to aneuploidy?

  5. Why is mitosis essential for multicellular organisms?

  6. Predict the consequences if sister chromatids failed to separate during meiosis II.
